title: Labhairt faoi mheabhráin / Talking about past experiences
bridge: In Irish, talking about past experiences often uses the past tense of the verb 'a bheith' (to be) for descriptive or continuous actions, unlike English where 'was/were' is used. Irish also uses the past tense of 'a dhéanamh' (to do) for completed actions, similar to English 'did'. Be careful with word order, as Irish places the verb before the subject in questions and negative sentences, which is different from English.
rule: To talk about past experiences in Irish, use the past tense of the verb. For descriptive or continuous actions, use the past tense of 'a bheith' (to be) + the verbal noun. For completed actions, use the past tense of 'a dhéanamh' (to do) + the verbal noun. Questions and negative sentences invert the word order, placing the verb before the subject. Common traps include incorrect verb conjugation and word order.

title: Socraigh / Making Arrangements
bridge: In Irish, making plans often involves more explicit expressions of intention and agreement compared to English. For instance, Irish uses specific verb forms like 'déanfaidh mé' (I will do) to confirm plans, whereas English might rely on simpler phrases like 'I'll do it'. Be cautious of false friends like 'plan' in English, which doesn’t directly translate to 'plean' in Irish for making arrangements; instead, use phrases like 'socraigh' or 'eagraigh'.
rule: To make plans in Irish, use the future tense with 'déanfaidh' (will do) followed by the verb. For suggestions, use 'cad faoi' (what about) or 'an dtiocfadh leat' (would you like). To confirm, use 'sea' (yes) or 'tá sé ceart' (that’s right). Negative responses can be expressed with 'ní' (not) before the verb, e.g., 'ní dtiocfaidh liom' (I can’t). Always use the correct pronoun for the subject, e.g., 'déanfaidh mé' (I will do), 'déanfaidh tú' (you will do).

title: Tabhair comhairle / Giving Advice
bridge: In Irish, giving advice often involves the use of the conditional tense, similar to English's 'should' or 'would'. However, Irish also uses the phrase 'ba cheart' (it would be right) which is more direct than English's 'you should'. Be careful not to overuse the English structure 'you should' directly, as it doesn't always translate well. Additionally, Irish advice can be more implicit, using phrases like 'is maith liom' (I like) to suggest a recommendation.
rule: To give advice in Irish, use the conditional tense of the verb or the phrase 'ba cheart duit' (you should) followed by the verbal noun. For example, 'Ba cheart duit an bus a thógáil' (You should take the bus). The conditional tense is formed by adding 'fá' or 'go' before the verb, e.g., 'fágfá' (you would leave). Exceptions include irregular verbs like 'bí' (to be), which becomes 'bheadh' in the conditional. Use 'is maith liom' (I like) for softer recommendations, e.g., 'Is maith liom an chóisir sin' (I like that restaurant).

title: Mo bharúil / Expressing Opinions
bridge: In Irish, expressing opinions often involves the phrase 'mo bharúil' (my opinion) or 'cheapas' (I think), which is more explicit than the English 'I think' or 'I believe'. English speakers might be tempted to directly translate 'I think' to 'cheapas', but in Irish, this phrase is often followed by the verbal noun (VN) form of the verb, which is different from the English infinitive. Additionally, Irish uses the eclipsis (n- prefix) after 'mo bharúil' with certain consonants, a feature absent in English.
rule: To express opinions in Irish, use 'mo bharúil' followed by the eclipsed verbal noun (VN) if the verb starts with p, t, or c, or 'go' + the verb in the subjunctive mood. For example, 'Mo bharúil go bhfuil...' (I think that...). Alternatively, use 'cheapas' + VN. Remember, the VN form is specific to each verb and must be learned individually. For instance, 'cheapas go mbeidh' (I think there will be).

title: Tá mé d’accord / Agreeing and Disagreeing
bridge: In Irish, agreeing and disagreeing often involve more explicit expressions compared to English. While English uses simple phrases like 'I agree' or 'I disagree', Irish frequently uses structures like 'Tá mé d’accord' (I agree) and 'Níl mé d’accord' (I disagree). Be cautious with false friends like 'd’accord', which is borrowed from French and not a native Irish word. Additionally, Irish often includes the subject pronoun explicitly, unlike English where it’s often omitted.
rule: To agree in Irish, use 'Tá mé d’accord' or 'Tá mé ar aghaidh [insert opinion]'. For disagreement, use 'Níl mé d’accord' or 'Níl mé ar aghaidh [insert opinion]'. The verb 'tá' (is) and 'níl' (is not) are essential here. Note that 'd’accord' is a direct loanword from French, and while commonly used, it’s not grammatically Irish. Native expressions like 'Tá mé ar aghaidh sin' (I am for that) are also used. Always include the subject pronoun (mé) for clarity.

title: Ag cur síos ar do rhutáin laethúla / Describing Your Daily Routine
bridge: In Irish, daily routines are often described using the present tense, similar to English. However, Irish uses a specific verbal noun structure with the word 'ag' (at) to indicate ongoing actions, which is a key difference from English. Be careful not to directly translate English phrases like 'I am doing' – instead, use 'Táim ag déanamh' (I am at doing). Also, Irish often omits the subject pronoun when the verb already indicates the subject, unlike English.
rule: To describe daily routines in Irish, use the structure 'Táim ag [verbal noun]' for 'I am [doing something]'. The verbal noun is formed by removing the 't-' from the verb's imperative form (e.g., 'déanamh' from 'déan'). For other subjects, use 'Tá [subject] ag [verbal noun]'. Remember, Irish often drops the subject pronoun when the verb conjugation makes it clear (e.g., 'Táim ag ithe' instead of 'Tá mé ag ithe').

title: Ag caint faoi shláinte / Talking about health
bridge: In Irish, discussing health and symptoms often involves more literal descriptions compared to English. For example, instead of saying 'I have a headache,' Irish uses a construction that translates to 'There is a pain in my head.' Be cautious of false friends like 'sláinte,' which means 'health' and not 'cheers' as in the common Irish toast borrowed into English.
rule: To talk about health and symptoms in Irish, use the phrase 'Tá [symptom] orm' for 'I have [symptom]' or 'Tá [symptom] agam.' For describing symptoms, use 'Tá [body part] ag déanamh [action],' e.g., 'Tá mo cheann ag tinneadh' (My head is aching). For general health, 'Tá mé [adjective]' is used, e.g., 'Tá mé slán' (I am healthy). Note that Irish often uses the verb 'bí' (to be) with the prepositional pronoun 'orm' or 'agam' to indicate possession of symptoms.

title: Déan iarratas / Making Requests
bridge: In Irish, making requests often involves the use of the verb 'déan' (do) followed by the prepositional pronoun 'le' (with) to address the person you're asking. This is quite different from English, where we typically use 'can you' or 'could you'. Be careful not to directly translate English phrases like 'Can you help me?' as Irish syntax and word order can vary. Additionally, Irish often uses the imperative form more frequently than English, so phrases like 'Tabhair dom' (Give me) are common and not considered rude.
rule: To make a request in Irish, use the structure 'Déan [le + person] [verb in the verbal noun form]'. For example, 'Déan le do chara cabhrú liom' (Do with your friend help me). The imperative form is also commonly used for direct requests, such as 'Tabhair dom an leabhar' (Give me the book). Remember that word order can be more flexible in Irish, but the verb often comes before the subject in questions or requests. Always use the correct prepositional pronouns (le, dom, duit, etc.) to address the person or indicate the recipient of the action.

title: Is féidir liom / I can
bridge: In Irish, expressing ability or possibility often uses the phrase 'Is féidir liom' (I can) or 'Is féidir' (It is possible). Unlike English, Irish does not use auxiliary verbs like 'can' or 'could' in the same way. Instead, 'Is féidir' remains unchanged regardless of the subject, which can be confusing for English speakers. Additionally, Irish often omits the subject pronoun when the context is clear, which is less common in English.
rule: To express ability or possibility in Irish, use 'Is féidir liom' for 'I can,' 'Is féidir leat' for 'You can,' and 'Is féidir leis' for 'He can,' etc. The structure is 'Is féidir + le + pronoun.' For general possibility, use 'Is féidir' followed by the verb in the verbal noun form. Note that 'Is féidir' does not change with tense or subject, unlike English 'can' or 'could.'

title: Ag caint faoi an aimsir / Talking about the weather
bridge: In Irish, talking about the weather often involves more descriptive phrases compared to English. For instance, Irish uses specific terms like 'ag cur báistí' (raining) instead of just 'raining'. Be cautious of false friends like 'fúinn' (humid), which doesn't directly translate to 'fun' in English. Additionally, Irish weather expressions often include the verb 'bí' (to be) in the present continuous tense, which is less common in English weather descriptions.
rule: To talk about the weather in Irish, use the present continuous tense of the verb 'bí' (to be) followed by the prepositional pronoun 'ag' and the verb describing the weather condition. For example, 'Tá sé ag cur báistí' (It is raining). Common weather verbs include 'cur báistí' (to rain), 'scaipeadh' (to clear up), and 'fúinn' (to be humid). Note that 'fúinn' is an adjective, so it follows the copula 'is' instead of 'ag'.
